conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes 'No', stating that high-certainty evidence indicates saw palmetto preparations do not improve urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia more than placebo over the longer term.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion: No.** The best available evidence indicates that saw palmetto (*Serenoa repens*) preparations do **not** improve urinary symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) more than placebo over the longer term.

A 2023 Cochrane review found **high-certainty evidence** of little to no difference in urinary-symptom scores at 12–17 months: mean difference 0.07 points on the International Prostate Symptom Score (95% CI −0.75 to 0.88; 3 studies, 898 participants). It also found little to no long-term quality-of-life difference (mean difference −0.11; 95% CI −0.41 to 0.19; 3 studies, 882 participants). These estimates are far below a clinically meaningful benefit.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia

This agrees with major placebo-controlled trials. In a year-long randomized trial, saw palmetto was not superior to placebo for urinary symptoms or objective BPH measures.  
https://escholarship.org/content/qt3d70w83q/qt3d70w83q.pdf

Likewise, in a 72-week dose-escalation trial, symptoms improved slightly in both groups—but not preferentially with saw palmetto: AUASI scores fell from 14.4 to 12.2 with extract and from 14.7 to 11.7 with placebo. Higher doses did not solve the problem.  
https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/668995

Small earlier studies sometimes suggested benefit, but larger, better-controlled trials and the systematic review outweigh that signal. NCCIH similarly concludes that a large high-dose study and Cochrane review found saw palmetto no more effective than placebo for BPH-related urinary symptoms.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto
